document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC to certain comments and protests re the PJM Reliability Backstop Procurement…

pages.text:
1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
) 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
 
 
) 
 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
) 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER  
AND ANSWER OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” 
or the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
(“Constellation”) respectfully moves for leave to answer and answers certain comments and 
protests filed in this proceeding (“Answer”). Constellation seeks to provide additional information 
and context that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process.2 
I. 
BACKGROUND 
On July 31, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) submitted revisions to the PJM 
Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among 
Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”).3  
 
1  18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213. 
2 Although the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure do not generally permit answers to answers unless 
otherwise ordered by the decisional authority, the Commission has made exceptions where an answer provides useful 
and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process, corrects factual inaccuracies 
and clarifies the issues, or assures a complete record in the proceeding. See, e.g., Pioneer Transmission, LLC v. N. 
Ind. Pub. Serv. Co., 140 FERC ¶ 61,057, at P 94 (2012) (accepting answers that “provided information that assisted 
us in our decision-making process”); Entergy Servs., Inc., 126 FERC ¶ 61,227, at P 76, order on clarification & reh’g, 
127 FERC ¶ 61,225 (2009); New Power Co. v. PJM Interconnection LLC, 98 FERC ¶ 61,208, at p. 61,756 (2002) 
(answer accepted to provide new factual and legal material to assist the Commission in decision-making process). 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming 
from Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (filed July 31, 2026) (the “PJM Proposal”).  Capitalized terms used 
but not otherwise defined herein have the meaning as defined in the Tariff, the RAA, or the PJM Proposal, as 
applicable.

2 
Numerous parties filed comments and protests addressing the proposal, including Constellation.4  
And many of these protests raised similar concerns, underscoring that the RBP as-proposed 
includes serious design flaws. 
II. 
ANSWER 
A. 
Request for Additional Clarification on Resources Eligible to Supply 
Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW 
Constellation maintains the arguments and requested relief set forth in its Limited Protest 
concerning the treatment of RBP Resources in subsequent RPM Auctions.5  The NRG Companies, 
the Independent Market Monitor for PJM, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (“NJBPU”), 
and the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel raised similar concerns regarding PJM’s 
mandatory price-taker requirement. Constellation will not repeat those arguments here but 
underscores the seriousness of this issue for market integrity going forward.6   
Constellation also maintains the arguments and requested relief for the limited 
modifications to other Tariff provisions described in its Limited Protest, with one additional 
clarification.  Constellation agrees with the sentiment expressed by other commenters that Section 
18.2 of the proposed Tariff, describing resources eligible to supply Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP 
 
4 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Limited Protest of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket No. ER26-3380-
000 (filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“Limited Protest”). 
5 See Limited Protest at 10–13. 
6 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Limited Protest of the NRG Companies, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 at 10–
11 (filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“[T]he proposed requirement that resources with RBP commitments offer as price-takers 
into RPM Auctions for the associated Delivery Years ‘is antithetical to creating a normal capacity market,’” and 
“‘send[s] the wrong signals [to] potential investors of PJM generation capacity.’”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 
Protest of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 at 11 (filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“Pay as 
bid is inefficient and does not facilitate competition.”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest and Request for Rejection 
of Filing or in the Alternative for Evidentiary Hearings and/or Settlement Proceedings by Office of the Ohio 
Consumers’ Counsel, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 at 7–8 (filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“OCC Protest”) (explaining that PJM 
has not supported the RBP’s proposed departure from the single clearing price approach to a pay-as-bid approach, 
which is “diametrically opposite what it has supported for over 20 years in its RPM auctions”); PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C., Comments of the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 at 5 (filed Aug. 21, 2026) 
(“NJBPU Comments”) (“[t]he Board has concerns that the pay-as-bid market structure, compared to PJM’s uniform 
clearing price in the capacity market, would create inefficient market outcomes or allow for market manipulation.”)

3 
MW, requires additional clarity and should be adjusted to avoid unintentionally “limiting [the] 
pool of qualifying resources.”7  Consistent with the request in Constellation’s Limited Protest with 
respect to resources qualifying as RBP Resources, the Commission should similarly condition 
acceptance of PJM’s RBP proposal on PJM revising the eligibility criteria for Qualifying RBP 
Offset UCAP MW.8  In particular, Energy Resources seeking new Capacity Interconnection Rights 
(CIRs) through an Interconnection Request should be able to satisfy the criteria for resources 
eligible to supply Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW.   
B. 
Credit and Collateral Requirements of Load Serving Entities 
The remainder of this Answer addresses the distinct load serving entity (“LSE”) credit and 
collateral issues raised in the responsive pleadings. Multiple commenters raised substantial 
concerns regarding PJM’s proposed LSE credit and collateral provisions. EKPC states that the 
magnitude of the proposed requirement “stands apart from anything in PJM’s experience.”9 
NOVEC characterizes the requirement as excessive and onerous.10 The NJBPU cautions that the 
size of the collateral requirement may challenge LSEs’ ability to obtain the required collateral and 
 
7 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest of Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc., Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
at 7–8 (filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“NOVEC Protest”); see also See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Comments of Equinix 
Inc. on the PJM Interconnection, LLC Filing Regarding its Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource 
Adequacy Concerns Stemming From Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 at 2 (filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“Equinix 
Comments”). 
8 See Limited Protest at 13–14 (requesting modifications to the proposed Tariff to add Energy Resources seeking new 
CIRs as a category of resource eligible under 18.5(b)(iii)(2) to qualify as an RBP Resource).  Notably, the PJM 
Proposal explained that “Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW has been deliberately designed to be more inclusive than 
the resources that qualify to sell RBP UCAP MW [i.e., RBP Resources].”  PJM Proposal at 42.  Because PJM has 
explicitly stated that the criteria for resources qualifying as RBP Resources are more restrictive, while the pool of 
Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW is intended to be more inclusive, it logically follows that the relief requested in 
Constellation’s Limited Protest extends to the criteria for resources eligible to supply Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP 
MW.  However, out of an abundance of caution, Constellation requests clarification and any necessary Tariff 
modifications to confirm that Energy Resources as described herein may also be eligible to supply Qualifying RBP 
Offset UCAP MW. 
9  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc., Docket No. ER26-3380-000 at 26 
(filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“EKPC Protest”) (citing Attachment 2, Affidavit of Carl F. Coscia at ¶ 61 (“Coscia Affidavit”)).  
10 NOVEC Protest at 3.

4 
observes that additional time would have permitted development of a more thoughtful collateral 
framework.11 
Constellation joins the chorus of voices raising concerns about the proposed LSE credit 
requirements.  The magnitude of the proposed collateral obligation for LSEs is enormous—it 
would rival the PJM credit holdings for all its markets combined.12 PJM proposes an initial RBP 
Credit Rate of $1.5 million for each MW of allocated RBP Obligation. Applied to the 6,831.3 MW 
Initial RBP Target, that rate could require LSEs collectively to post approximately $10.2 billion 
in collateral. In his Affidavit to the EKPC Protest, Mr. Carl Coscia puts this figure in context, 
noting that “PJM’s monthly Key Risk Metrics reporting shows the total collateral PJM holds from 
all Members, against every market it operates, at approximately $6.2 billion on average in 2025 
and $7.0 billion in 2025,” and approximately $10.9 billion as of July 30, 2026.13 
Importantly, the approximately $10.2 billion collateral estimate captures only collateral 
posted by LSEs to PJM. It does not capture the additional credit support that LSEs are almost 
certain to require from the large-load customers whose obligations they serve. In other words, if 
an LSE is required to post significant collateral to PJM as a result of its large load retail customer, 
the LSE is likely to then require its large load retail customer to provide the same or similar 
collateral to the LSE, more or less doubling the total collateral required for an RBP customer.  
Given the magnitude of the collateral PJM proposes to require LSEs to post, this “double 
collateral” problem will strain liquidity and add significantly to already-significant financing and 
transaction costs. 
 
11 NJBPU Comments at 5-6. 
12 Coscia Aff. ¶ 63. 
13 Id. (emphasis added).

5 
As discussed below, Constellation (1) has significant concerns about the fixed $1.5 
million/MW RBP Credit Rate and believes it is excessive; (2) suggests, to address the “double 
collateral issue,” that the applicable large-load customer should be permitted to post qualifying 
collateral directly for the account of the responsible LSE; and (3) given these concerns and similar 
concerns raised by other parties, requests that the Commission sever and/or defer proposed Tariff 
section 18.8(b) for resolution on an expedited paper hearing with a short timeline (about 125 days) 
for resolution without delaying the RBP solicitation or the seller-side credit requirements. 
1. 
PJM’s Fixed $1.5 Million/MW Rate Is Based on Contract Notional, 
Not Measured Credit Exposure 
PJM has a legitimate interest in protecting the RBP against reasonably foreseeable 
nonpayment. But the amount of collateral imposed on LSEs must bear a reasoned relationship to 
the exposure being secured. PJM has not made that showing for its fixed $1.5 million/MW rate, 
and it is not “reasonably tailored to the actual credit risk presented”14 nor “derived from measured 
exposure.”15 
PJM derives the proposed rate from approximately one-half of the gross notional value of 
a hypothetical fifteen-year RBP commitment priced at $555/MW-day. PJM also performs a 
discounted-cash-flow calculation using the capacity-market weighted average cost of capital. 
Those calculations explain how PJM arrived at the $1.5 million figure. They do not demonstrate 
 
14 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest of FirstEnergy Service Company, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 at 8 (filed Aug. 
21, 2026). 
15 EKPC Protest at 23.

6 
that the figure measures reasonably foreseeable credit exposure. And discounting a gross payment 
stream does not convert it into a credit-exposure analysis. 
The methodology has five material gaps. First, it assumes that every committed RBP 
megawatt is priced at the $555/MW-day maximum willingness to pay, although accepted RBP 
prices may be lower and may vary by resource and Delivery Year. Second, it uses fifteen years of 
gross contract value rather than the net RBP Charges that LSEs actually will be billed, should RBP 
Resources not be segregated from the market. Third, it does not identify the period of unpaid 
charges to be secured, the time needed to draw collateral and reallocate any residual default, or the 
stress assumptions used to estimate net exposure. Fourth, it applies the same $1.5 million/MW 
base rate without explaining why credit quality may increase—but never reduce—the base 
requirement. Finally, although PJM may reduce the rate over time, the proposed Tariff establishes 
no mandatory recalculation schedule, prescribed inputs, or objective collateral-release standard. 
PJM’s proposed default rule further demonstrates the disconnect. Proposed Tariff section 
18.9(a) provides that an unpaid RBP Charge will be reallocated to the remaining LSEs responsible 
for RBP Charges and that the defaulting LSE’s RBP Collateral may be applied as an offset. PJM 
does not explain why the exposure arising before collateral can be drawn and any residual default 
reallocated should be measured by one-half of a fifteen-year gross payment stream. 
Assuming for the sake of argument that it is accepted, the PJM-proposed contract-for-
differences settlement further illustrates the mismatch. If the Commission rejects Constellation’s 
proposal to segregate RBP Resources and associated load from RPM and accepts PJM’s proposal, 
the payment due to RBP Resources in any Delivery Year will only equal the amount that the RBP 
Resources do not recover from RPM, which already has its own credit and collateral obligations. 
EKPC calculates that, at the $555/MW-day maximum willingness to pay and the Initial RBP

7 
Target, one year of gross RBP payments would be approximately $1.38 billion. Using the 
$325/MW-day clearing price from the 2028/2029 BRA, EKPC calculates a first-year net payment 
of approximately $573 million. The proposed $10.2 billion collateral requirement would equal 
approximately 740% of one year’s gross commitment value, and approximately 1,790% of the 
amount actually billed to load ($573 million).16 
Those comparisons are illustrative. Neither a one-year exposure horizon nor the $325/MW-
day clearing price necessarily supplies the appropriate collateral standard for future Delivery 
Years. But the comparisons demonstrate why a fixed percentage of the maximum fifteen-year 
gross notional value is not a reasoned measure of payment exposure.17 
The Commission should not replace PJM’s unsupported methodology with another 
mechanical shortcut.  In particular, if RBP Resources become price-takers in RPM, the 
replacement RBP Credit Rate should not simply equal $555/MW-day less a single assumed future 
RPM price. A revised methodology should account for the actual accepted RBP prices and 
quantities; the net settlement structure, if accepted by the Commission; a defined default-
management and reallocation horizon; reasoned stress assumptions for future net RBP Charges; 
applicable LSE or guarantor credit quality; qualifying collateral or guarantees already held by 
 
16 EKPC Protest at 25 (emphasis added). 
17 See Coscia Aff. ¶ 187 (“The $1.5 million per MW Credit Rate does not depend on the credit quality of the LSE, a 
recalculation of Peak Market Activity or expected exposure, or the use of other mitigation tools to address an identified 
deficiency. It applies the same fixed rate per megawatt before unsecured credit to every LSE subject to section 18.8(b), 
regardless of those considerations.”).

8 
PJM; and mandatory periodic recalculation and release standards. Any change the Commission 
accepts to the RBP settlement structure should be reflected in the collateral methodology. 
2. 
Large Load Customers Should Be Permitted to Post Collateral for the 
Account of the Responsible LSE  
An excessive collateral requirement can create the very liquidity risk it is intended to 
mitigate. Under the filed design, an LSE must furnish RBP Collateral to PJM or PJMSettlement 
and may then prudently obtain corresponding support from the large-load customer associated with 
the obligation. That structure can encumber two balance sheets and impose two layers of financing 
and transaction costs for the same payment obligation. 
The Tariff therefore should permit the applicable large load customer, or an affiliate acting 
on its behalf, to post RBP Collateral directly with PJM or PJMSettlement for the account of the 
responsible LSE. The LSE should remain fully responsible for payment of RBP Charges; PJM or 
PJMSettlement should have direct and unconditional draw rights; and the customer-posted amount 
should satisfy the LSE’s collateral requirement dollar-for-dollar. The same collateral should not 
be credited against more than one obligation, and disputes between the customer and the LSE 
should not impair PJM’s draw rights. 
This option would not reduce PJM’s credit protection or change the entity responsible for 
paying RBP Charges. It would add the option for another entity18 to furnish the collateral and 
thereby avoid unnecessary intermediation through the LSE and duplicative credit postings. In 
addition to the advantages described above, allowing the large load to post collateral will facilitate 
a seamless transition if the customer changes its LSE, the applicable RBP Obligation changes, or 
 
18 Importantly, the proposed modification to the Tariff would permit a large load customer to post RBP Collateral 
directly with PJM or PJMSettlement, but would not require such an arrangement.

9 
the posting arrangement otherwise terminates.19 
3. 
The Commission Can Preserve the RBP Procurement Schedule While 
Resolving the LSE Collateral Provisions in an Expedited Paper 
Hearing  
The procurement is urgent; the future LSE collateral methodology is not. RBP Sellers must 
satisfy the seller-side credit requirements in connection with their RBP Sell Offers. By contrast, 
the first LSE collateral requirement will not arise, as currently proposed, until forty-five days 
before the 2028/2029 Delivery Year. The Commission therefore can accept the RBP solicitation, 
selection process, commitments, and seller-side credit provisions while severing or deferring its 
decision on only proposed Tariff section 18.8(b). That disposition would not displace 
Constellation’s separate request in its Limited Protest that the initial RBP Obligation allocations 
be determined 365 days before the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.20 
The present record is sufficient to conclude that PJM has not supported the fixed $1.5 
million/MW rate. The record is not sufficiently developed, however, to prescribe a durable 
replacement methodology.21  The replacement must be conformed to the RBP settlement structure 
accepted by the Commission and supported by evidence addressing the relevant exposure horizon, 
stress assumptions, credit-quality treatment, customer-posted collateral, collateral already held by 
PJM, switching and transfer mechanics, and mandatory recalculation and release standards. 
 
19 See, e.g., NOVEC Protest at 24 (“The Commission should require PJM to allow other methods to demonstrate 
creditworthiness besides posting the full collateral or a letter of credit.”); Equinix Comments at 2 (RBP collateral 
provisions should be revised to “calibrate[] to reasonably foresee forward exposure” and revise “the forms of credit 
support” required).  
20 See Limited Protest at 16–17. 
21 See, e.g., OCC Protest (requesting evidentiary hearings and/or settlement proceedings to adequately consider the 
RBP); NOVEC Protest at 4–9; NJBPU Comments at 5–6 (“[T]he Board is concerned that the size of the collateral 
requirements may make it difficult for LSEs to secure the required collateral . . . . While the Board does not provide 
a solution at this time, the Board and stakeholders could have used additional time to build a more thoughtful collateral 
system.”).

10 
Given that required credit support will not be posted until sometime in April 2028, there is 
time to consider a “more thoughtful collateral system.”22 The Commission, therefore, should 
establish an expedited paper hearing limited to proposed Tariff section 18.8(b). Within thirty days 
after the later of the Commission’s order or PJM’s publication of the final RBP commitments, PJM 
should file a proposed revised LSE collateral methodology and supporting analysis. Initial briefs 
should be due twenty days thereafter, and reply briefs fifteen days after the initial briefs. 
Constellation requests that the Commission issue an order within sixty days after the close of 
briefing. 
This schedule would produce a complete record approximately 125 days after the relevant 
RBP commitments and well before any LSE collateral must be posted. It also would leave the RBP 
procurement and seller-side credit protections undisturbed. 
Setting the credit requirement and mechanism issues in a separate expedited track to 
evaluate and form consensus for the collateralization requirements will help ensure the cost 
allocation methodology keeps the RBP costs with large loads and not residential customers, 
properly sizes collateral requirements commensurate with exposure and credit risk, and considers 
alternative solutions to credit support that will help alleviate the incredible burden faced by LSEs, 
particularly smaller entities. The current record and procedural schedule is not adequate to address 
the necessary details of the credit and collateral requirements. 
 
 
 
22 NJBPU Comments at 6.

11 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
In accordance with PJM’s willingness to accept changes under NRG Power Marketing,23 
the Commission should (i) accept the RBP subject to the modifications Constellation discussed in 
its Limited Protest in this proceeding, with the additional clarification discussed above permitting 
Energy Resources seeking new capacity rights to satisfy the criteria for resources eligible to supply 
Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, and (ii) sever the LSE credit issue discussed herein for further 
proceedings and refer that issue to an expedited paper hearing. 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
Dated: September 8, 2026 
 
23 See PJM Proposal at 3 (“PJM provides notice that it consents to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify 
and/or sever any element of the proposed Tariff and RAA language to the extent necessary and permitted under section 
205 of the FPA and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC, where such modification and/or severance is consistent 
with PJM’s overarching objectives in this filing”).
